sentences.text: Changzhousaurus possessed large wings on its forelimbs and smaller wings on its hindlimbs.
Its mouth contained around twenty unserrated teeth, with the front ones being slender and close together, while the rear teeth were robust and widely spaced.
The forelimb was proportionately long, measuring about sixty percent the length of the hindlimb.
An enlarged claw on the second toe was seven and a half millimeters long, with a keratin sheath adding another four and a half millimeters.
Feathers covered the body, ranging from ten to thirty-five millimeters over the head and neck, twenty to thirty millimeters on the tail base, and up to sixty millimeters on the lower legs.
Fossils of this animal were discovered in the Jiufotang Formation in western Liaoning Province, China.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — included nine cervical vertebrae, though ten were likely present.
The individual represented by the holotype was likely not a juvenile but had not reached full maturity when it died.
Its femur was bowed forward and shorter than the tibia, and impressions of keratin sheaths are preserved around the hand and foot claws.
Changzhousaurus is classified as a pennaraptoran theropod displaying a mosaic of features, possibly representing an early-diverging deinonychosaurian.
Xu (2026) placed Changzhousaurus within Deinonychosauria as an early-diverging member to support the monophyly of that group.
This creature lived during the Early Cretaceous Aptian period, between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether dromaeosaurids and troodontids form a single monophyletic clade called Deinonychosauria.
